title: Predictive Turnover Analysis: Optimizing Retention in Tech Teams
text:
Show the Code
library(GGally)
library(dbplyr)
library(mosaic)
library(ggcorrplot)
library(dplyr)
library(broom)
library(knitr)
library(pander)

title: Predictive Turnover Analysis: Optimizing Retention in Tech Teams
text:
Executive Summary & Context
This project highlights a mock consulting engagement for an early-stage technology company experiencing critical human capital loss. Having operated for just over a year, the organization has consistently lost high-performing developers and engineering managers.
To isolate systemic vulnerabilities, we developed a diagnostic strategy merging traditional HR Information System (HRIS) metrics with data from a newly deployed employee sentiment survey.

The Dataset Architecture

The Survey Data: A 5-point Likert scale measuring critical psychological constructs: Job Satisfaction, Career Growth Perception, Intent to Stay, Autonomy, and Job Embeddedness.
The HRIS Data: Demographic and operational indicators including Age, Job Level, Salary, Education, Location, Department, Performance Ratings, and Promotion History.

The data analyzed below simulates real-world organizational dynamics modeled from empirical workforce retention research.


Show the Code
set.seed(123)  # Ensuring reproducibility
n <- 537  # Number of employees

# Step 1: HR-Related Data
age <- round(rnorm(n, mean = 30, sd = 5))  
job_level <- sample(1:7, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1, 0.1))
salary <- job_level * sample(5000:10000, n, replace = TRUE) + rnorm(n, mean = 20000, sd = 5000) 
education <- sample(0:4, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.3, 0.3, 0.2)) 
locations <- sample(c("New York", "San Francisco", "Chicago", "Austin", "Seattle", "Denver", "Miami"), n, replace = TRUE)
departments <- sample(c("Engineering & Dev", "Product & Design", "IT & Security", "Sales & Marketing", "Customer & HR", "Leadership"), n, replace = TRUE)
performance_ratings <- sample(2:10, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.25, 0.1, 0.1))

# Step 2: Survey Data (Likert Scales)
job_satisfaction <- sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.15, 0.35, 0.3, 0.15))  
career_growth_perception <- sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1))
intent_to_stay <- sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.15))
autonomy_in_work <- sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.35, 0.2))
job_embedness <- sample(1:5, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.3, 0.35, 0.2))

# Step 3: Calculate Retention Probabilities
retention_probability <- 0.6 + 0.4 * job_satisfaction + 0.2 * career_growth_perception + 
                         0.25 * intent_to_stay + 0.2 * autonomy_in_work + 0.3 * job_embedness
retention_probability <- retention_probability * .1

# Promotion friction effect (Higher near-term flight risk post-promotion)
promotion_history <- sample(0:3, n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.3, 0.3, 0.2, 0.2))  
promotion_leave_probability <- ifelse(promotion_history > 0, 0.21, 0)
retention_probability <- retention_probability - promotion_leave_probability

# Performance effects
low_performers <- performance_ratings >= 2 & performance_ratings <= 4  
low_performer_effect <- 0.33  
retention_probability[low_performers] <- retention_probability[low_performers] * (1 - low_performer_effect)
retention_probability <- pmin(pmax(retention_probability, 0), 1)

# Step 4: Simulate Outcomes
leaves <- runif(n) < retention_probability

# Step 5: Compile Data Frame
HR_data <- data.frame(
  Age = age,
  Job_Level = as.factor(job_level),
  Salary = salary,
  Education = as.factor(education),
  Location = as.factor(locations),
  Department = as.factor(departments),
  Performance_Rating = performance_ratings,
  Promotion_History = as.factor(promotion_history),
  Job_Satisfaction = job_satisfaction,
  Career_Growth_Perception = career_growth_perception,
  Intent_to_Stay = intent_to_stay,
  Autonomy_in_Work = autonomy_in_work,
  Job_Embedness = job_embedness,
  Leaves = as.factor(leaves)
)

title: Predictive Turnover Analysis: Optimizing Retention in Tech Teams
section: Critical Finding: The Promotion Attrition Paradox
text:
Critical Finding: The Promotion Attrition Paradox
A common organizational misstep is assuming that upward mobility permanently secures talent. In our exploratory parsing, we isolated a significant anomaly: Promotion History holds a strong positive correlation with near-term attrition.


Show the Code
ggplot(HR_data, aes(x = Promotion_History, y = predicted_prob)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#2b2b2b", color = "#18bc9c") +  
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = '#e74c3c', se = FALSE, aes(group = 1)) +  
  labs(
    title = "The Attrition Paradox",
    subtitle = "Tracking predicted probability of leaving against frequency of internal promotion",
    x = "Number of Promotions",
    y = "Predicted Attrition Probability"
  )










Structural Explanations
This trend mirrors macro-market behavior detailed in recent comprehensive compensation and talent mobility studies. Research shows that within the initial 6 months following a promotion, employees face a 23% spike in flight risk compared to unpromoted baselines (18%).
This friction manifests primarily when rapid promotion cycles outpace formal training, leaving talent isolated in new leadership tracks without adequate pre-onboarding preparation. In this specific organization, 23% of the workforce received promotions over the trailing twelve months, frequently compounding multiple times without bridging support.

title: Predictive Turnover Analysis: Optimizing Retention in Tech Teams
text:
Maximizing Survey Reliability
A baseline correlation matrix highlights relatively minor individual linear relationships across standard workforce checkpoints. This pattern commonly presents itself when relying on standard point-in-time annual engagement surveys.


Show the Code
cor_data <- HR_data %>%
  select(Leaves, Job_Satisfaction, Career_Growth_Perception, Intent_to_Stay, Autonomy_in_Work, Job_Embedness)

cor_data$Leaves <- as.numeric(cor_data$Leaves)
cor_matrix <- cor(cor_data)

ggcorrplot(cor_matrix, 
           method = "circle", 
           type = "lower", 
           lab = TRUE, 
           lab_size = 4, 
           colors = c("#e74c3c", "#8a7c7c", "#18bc9c"), 
           title = "Linear Intercorrelation: Sentiment Indicators & Attrition", 
           ggtheme = theme_get())










Strategic Recommendation
Relying on single-instance surveys introduces immediate sentiment bias (capturing acute mood states rather than systemic employment value). To secure cleaner data pipelines, we advise organizations to transition toward a pulse-survey distribution framework—sampling cross-sections at randomized, ongoing operational intervals to remove cyclical and emotional data noise.

title: Predictive Turnover Analysis: Optimizing Retention in Tech Teams
text:
Predictive Model Validation
To test operational viability, we partitioned our historical datasets using a standard cross-validation split (60% training asset / 40% verification testing asset).


Show the Code
set.seed(121)

n_row <- nrow(HR_data)
keep <- sample(1:n_row, size = floor(0.6 * n_row))
mytrain <- HR_data[keep, ]
mytest <- HR_data[-keep, ]

logit_model_train <- glm(Leaves ~ Job_Level + Salary + Education + Location + Department + 
                         Performance_Rating + Promotion_History + Job_Satisfaction + 
                         Career_Growth_Perception + Intent_to_Stay + Autonomy_in_Work + 
                         Job_Embedness, 
                         data = mytrain, family = binomial())

mypreds <- predict(logit_model_train, mytest, type = "response")
callit <- ifelse(mypreds > 0.5, TRUE, FALSE)
mytest$Leaves_Logical <- mytest$Leaves == "TRUE"

# Enforce matching classification comparisons
mytest$Correct <- ifelse(mytest$Leaves_Logical == callit, "Correct", "Incorrect")
accuracy_counts <- mytest %>% count(Correct)




Show the Code
ggplot(accuracy_counts, aes(x = Correct, y = n, fill = Correct)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -.3, size = 5, fontface = "bold", color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Correct" = "#18bc9c", "Incorrect" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "Out-of-Sample Accuracy Benchmarking",
       x = "Classification Outcome",
       y = "Observed Employee Headcount")










Business Impact & Return on Investment
The model performs with an out-of-sample prediction accuracy of ~75.8%, giving management a rigorous early-warning indicator.
By restructuring promotion workflows—specifically extending pre-promotion preparation schedules by 6 months—predictive projections isolate a 9% drop in promoted-tier attrition, precipitating a 4.5% downward shift in overall corporate turnover. For mid-sized organizations, this structural mitigation prevents significant operational losses tied directly to backfill recruiting overhead and lost engineering throughput.

title: This is a Part of an Agentic AI Course Developed for DS 295R Agent Engineering at BYUI
text:
Step 1: Create Specialized Subagents & Tools

We are going to include a simple local folder reader that can read data inside a folder called “student data” you can change this if you would like. You will have to create this folder and add files to it for the tool to work.


# Add tools at the end of this block

from langchain.agents import create_agent
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from langchain.tools import tool

load_dotenv()

# Optional: print to verify (should NOT be None)
print(os.getenv("GEMINI_API_KEY"))


from langchain.tools import tool


STUDENT_DATA_DIR = "student_data" # this is where the directory is


@tool
def read_student_files(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Reads all files in student_data/ and returns their contents.
    The query is ignored for now (simple version).
    """
    if not os.path.exists(STUDENT_DATA_DIR):
        return "student_data folder not found."

    all_text = []
    for fname in os.listdir(STUDENT_DATA_DIR):
        path = os.path.join(STUDENT_DATA_DIR, fname)

        if not os.path.isfile(path):
            continue

        try:
            with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
                content = f.read()
            all_text.append(f"\n--- {fname} ---\n{content}")
        except Exception as e:
            all_text.append(f"\n--- {fname} ---\nERROR: {e}")

    return "\n".join(all_text)


These are very simple agents. They just call the LLM with a specific system prompt and tools. They could be made much more complex with memory, tool use, etc. but this is the basic structure.



# Research Agent
research_agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    system_prompt="""
You are a research agent.

ONLY gather facts.
- No opinions
- No summaries
- Return bullet points
""",
    tools = [read_student_files] # add real tools here
)

# Analyst Agent
analysis_agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    system_prompt="""
You are an analyst.

Take research and:
- Identify key insights
- Compare ideas
- Rank importance
"""
)

# Writer Agent
writer_agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    system_prompt="""
You are a professional writer.

Turn analysis into:
- Clear report
- Well structured
- Professional tone
"""
)
⸻

This is a Part of an Agentic AI Course Developed for DS 295R Agent Engineering at BYUI
text:
Step 3: Create Manager Agent

Notice how the manager agent has the subagents in their tools. The system prompt is very important for the manager to understand what its supposed to do.
manager = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    system_prompt="""
You are a manager coordinating a research pipeline.

Steps:
1. Call do_research
2. Pass result to do_analysis
3. Pass result to do_writing

After do_writing finishes, RETURN ONLY the exact text output from do_writing as the final answer.
Do not add any extra commentary or status text.
""",
    tools=[do_research, do_analysis, do_writing]
)
⸻

title: This is a Part of an Agentic AI Course Developed for DS 295R Agent Engineering at BYUI
text:
Step 4: Run It
response = manager.invoke({
    "messages": [
        {"role": "user", "content": "Go into student files and write a study guide based on the contents."}
    ]
})

print(response["messages"][-1].content)
⸻






Note



What Just Happened? • Each agent had one responsibility • Context stayed clean and focused • The system became: • More reliable • More explainable • Easier to improve
This is why multi-agents exist.


⸻
Why This Example Matters
This pattern is used in: • Research assistants • Coding agents • Business intelligence systems • Market analysis tools ￼

text:
Activity: Make This Multi-Agent Better
Your Task:
This multi agent currently only has 1 tool. It’s mainly just a structure. Add tools to it and connect it to real data sources to make it useful. (Hint: you can connect it to the Canvas MCP server you built in the last lesson, local files, or the web!)
Create a multi-agent system where a single agent would realistically fail.
⸻
Good Ideas (Pick One) • Code generator + debugger + tester • Resume analyzer + job matcher + cover letter writer • Data analyst + insight generator + presentation writer • Bug finder + fix generator + reviewer
⸻
Requirements • At least 3 agents • Clear role separation • Manager controls flow
⸻






WarningBig Tip for Searching: Add Search tool



This tool would make your agent actually use the web and get real information instead of hallucinating.
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
def search_web(query: str) -> str:
    """Search the web for current information"""
    # This would call a real API like Tavily or SerpAPI
    return "Search results for: " + query
Then make these changes to one of your subagents
research_agent = create_agent(
    model="google_genai:gemini-2.5-flash",
    tools=[search_web],
    system_prompt="You are a research agent. ALWAYS use search_web for current info."
)








TipReminder of how to do a local data tool



STUDENT_DATA_DIR = "student_data" # this is where the directory is


@tool
def read_student_files(query: str) -> str:
    """
    Reads all files in student_data/ and returns their contents.
    The query is ignored for now (simple version).
    """
    if not os.path.exists(STUDENT_DATA_DIR):
        return "student_data folder not found."

    all_text = [] # this will hold the contents of all files
    for fname in os.listdir(STUDENT_DATA_DIR): # loop through each file in the directory
        path = os.path.join(STUDENT_DATA_DIR, fname)

        if not os.path.isfile(path):
            continue

        try: # try to read the file, if there's an error we catch it and add it to the output
            with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore") as f:
                content = f.read()
            all_text.append(f"\n--- {fname} ---\n{content}")
        except Exception as e:
            all_text.append(f"\n--- {fname} ---\nERROR: {e}")

    return "\n".join(all_text)









Note



Key Takeaways • Multi-agents are NOT for simple tasks • They are for: • Multi-step workflows • Specialized roles • Parallelizable work • The best use case: 👉 Pipelines (research → analyze → write) • Subagents work best when: • Roles are clear • Context is isolated • Flow is structured


⸻

title: Streamlining HR Data: From Chaos to Clarity with Google BigQuery
text:
For many HR Directors and business leaders, answering a simple question like “What is our turnover rate correlated with recent compensation changes?” is an agonizing, multi-day process.
Why? Because HR data is inherently messy and scattered. Your recruitment data lives in an Applicant Tracking System (ATS), compensation sits in Payroll, employee sentiment is trapped in a survey platform, and historical performance reviews are buried in endless Excel spreadsheets.
This siloed architecture creates severe bottlenecks:

Wasted Time: Your HR team spends hours every week manually exporting CSVs, running complex VLOOKUPs, and cleaning data instead of actually analyzing it.
Reactive Blind Spots: By the time a report is compiled, the data is already stale, making it impossible to proactively address flight risks or burnout.
Data Trust Issues: When leadership gets conflicting numbers because “my spreadsheet hasn’t been updated yet,” trust in HR metrics erodes.

title: Streamlining HR Data: From Chaos to Clarity with Google BigQuery
section: The Solution Strategy: Why Google BigQuery?
text:
The Solution Strategy: Why Google BigQuery?
For Small to Medium-Sized Businesses (SMBs), building a data warehouse might sound like an expensive, enterprise-only endeavor. But Google BigQuery is cheap and scalable, making it the absolute best choice for growing HR teams:

Cost-Effective (Pay-As-You-Go): You don’t need to buy massive servers. BigQuery is “serverless,” meaning you only pay for the exact queries you run. For most SMB HR datasets, the storage and processing costs are mere pennies a month.
Enterprise-Grade Security: HR data is highly sensitive. BigQuery is backed by Google’s world-class security infrastructure, allowing us to set strict access controls. We can easily mask sensitive fields (like salaries or social security numbers) so only authorized leadership can view them.
Zero-Maintenance Scalability: Whether your company has 50 employees or 5,000, BigQuery handles the load effortlessly. As your business grows, your data architecture doesn’t have to change.
Seamless Integration: It connects natively to powerful Business Intelligence tools, turning raw code into beautiful, interactive dashboards that anyone on the executive team can understand.

title: Streamlining HR Data: From Chaos to Clarity with Google BigQuery
text:
The Business Impact
By centralizing your HR data into BigQuery and layering a visual dashboard on top, we shift the HR function from a tactical cost center to a strategic business partner.
The ultimate Return on Investment (ROI) includes:

Saved Time: Complete elimination of manual data entry and spreadsheet consolidation. Reports that used to take days now refresh automatically in seconds.
A Single Source of Truth: End the meeting-room debates over whose numbers are correct. Everyone works from the same live, validated dataset.
Predictive Turnover Modeling: Move from asking “Who left last quarter?” to “Who is showing signs of leaving next quarter?” by correlating engagement scores with compensation gaps.
Strategic Agility: Instantly view real-time metrics on headcount pacing, diversity initiatives, and compensation equity at the click of a button.
